t.1.112.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, O great king, Kuntī then spoke to Pāṇḍu, her husband, the lord of the earth, the heroic bull among the Kurus.
t.1.112.2: O knower of dharma, you should not speak to me in this way at all, O lotus-eyed one, to me, your lawful wife, who is devoted to you.
t.1.112.3: But you alone, O mighty-armed Bhārata, O hero, will beget on me, in accordance with dharma, children endowed with valor.
t.1.112.5: For I would not go, even in thought, to any other man but you. And what other human being on earth is more excellent than you?
t.1.112.4: O tiger among men, may I go to heaven together with you; and you yourself, O joy of the Kurus, come to me for the sake of offspring.
t.1.112.7: Long ago, it is said, there was a king known as Vyuṣitāśva, supremely devoted to dharma, who increased the lineage of Pūru.
t.1.112.6: Meanwhile, O large-eyed one, hear from me this righteous and ancient tale, a famous one, which I shall now relate.
t.1.112.8: And while that righteous, great-souled one was performing the sacrifice, the gods, with Indra at their head, came there together with the great ṛṣis.
t.1.112.9: Then, at the sacrifice of the great-souled royal seer Vyuṣitāśva, Indra grew intoxicated with soma, and the twice-born were gladdened by the sacrificial gifts.
t.1.112.10: Then, O king, Vyuṣitāśva shone forth surpassing all mortals, just as the sun at the passing of winter outshines all beings.
t.1.112.11: Having conquered and seized the kings of the east, the north, the middle lands and the south, that best of kings drove them before him.
t.1.112.12: At the great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice, the mighty Vyuṣitāśva became, indeed, a lord among kings, endowed with the strength of ten elephants.
t.1.112.13: And on this matter those people who know the ancient lore sing a verse: Vyuṣitāśva, having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean, protected all the classes as a father protects the sons of his own body.
t.1.112.14: Sacrificing with great sacrifices, he gave wealth to the brāhmaṇas; taking up endless jewels, he performed great rites. He pressed out many soma offerings and carried out the soma ceremonies.
t.1.112.16: The two of them loved each other passionately, so tradition says; and he, intoxicated with desire for her, fell into a wasting consumption.
t.1.112.15: And he had a greatly esteemed wife, Kākṣīvatī, named Bhadrā, O lord of men, who was unequalled in beauty on earth.
t.1.112.18: O tiger among men, we have heard that Bhadrā, sonless and afflicted with the deepest grief, lamented; hear that, O lord of men.
t.1.112.17: Because of that, within a short time he went to his setting like the sun. When that lord of men had died, his wife, deeply grief-stricken,
t.1.112.21: Bereft of you, I cannot bear to live even for a moment. Grant me your grace, O king, and lead me swiftly away from here.
t.1.112.20: For a woman without her husband, death is better, O bull among kṣatriyas. I wish to go the way you have gone; be gracious and lead me.
t.1.112.19: O you who know the highest dharma, every woman bereft of sons who lives on without her husband does not truly live; she is only wretched.
t.1.112.22: I shall follow behind you, O tiger among men, on level ground and on rough, as you go forth never to return.
t.1.112.23: Like a shadow that never departs, O king, I shall always be obedient to your will; O tiger among men, I shall ever delight in what is dear and beneficial to you.
t.1.112.24: From this day on, O king, without you, O lotus-eyed one, grievous anxieties that wither the heart will overpower me.
t.1.112.26: This sorrow born of separation from you, O king, has come upon me, heaped up by wicked deeds done in former bodies.
t.1.112.25: Surely, O king, in my former bodies I, unfortunate woman that I am, separated companions from one another, or broke apart those who were united.
t.1.112.27: From this day forth, O king, I shall lie upon a bed of kuśa grass, overcome by sorrow, wholly intent on seeing you again.
t.1.112.30: Rise, good lady, and go; here I grant you a boon: I will beget offspring in you, O sweetly smiling one.
t.1.112.29: As she lamented thus in many ways, again and again, clasping that corpse in her embrace, a voice, it is said, spoke from out of sight.
t.1.112.28: O tiger among men, kindly show yourself to me, who am filled with sorrow, wretched, without a protector, pitiable and lamenting, O lord of men.
t.1.112.31: And, O lovely-hipped one, having bathed after your season, you should lie with me upon your own bed on the fourteenth or the eighth day of the lunar fortnight.
t.1.112.32: Thus addressed, that devoted wife, the queen Bhadrā, desiring a son, then did just as she had been told, carrying out those words exactly as they were spoken.
t.1.112.33: By that corpse, O lord of men, the queen gave birth to sons, three Śālvas and four Madras, O best of the Bharatas.
t.1.112.34: Likewise you too, O bull among the Bharatas, are able to beget sons on me by your mind alone, through the power of your austerity and yoga.
